title: ‘Mite’ once sounded like ‘meet’: the vowels moved, the spelling didn’t
body: Between roughly 1400 and 1700, every long vowel of English changed in the **Great Vowel Shift**, starting in southern England. The two highest, /iː/ in bite and /uː/ in out, broke into two-part vowels, while the others were raised a step, so Middle English mite sounded much like today’s meet. English spelling was starting to settle in the 15th and 16th centuries and did not follow the changes, which is the main reason English vowel letters no longer sound as they do in Italian or German.

slides.prompt: Around 1400, the Middle English word ‘mite’ sounded similar to which modern English word?
slides.detail: Its long i was pronounced /iː/. Over the next three centuries the long vowels shifted, but the spelling stayed put.

slides.alt: Pastel diagram of the mouth with a vowel chart inside: seven words move from 1400 to 1900. Bite and out break into gliding vowels, meet and boot rise, then mate, meat and boat rise a step; the spelling b-i-t-e stays while its vowel goes from /iː/ to /aɪ/; German respells bīzen as beißen.
slides.music: “Sheep May Safely Graze - BWV 208” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Slide from 1400 to 1900 and watch seven long vowels move up the mouth, while their spellings stay the same.
slides.takeaway: The high vowels of bite and out became glides; meet and boot rose into their place, and later mate, meat and boat rose a step. The spellings stayed put, so they still show the old vowels.

slides.heading: Two phases
slides.text: By about 1500, /iː/ and /uː/ in bite and out had become diphthongs, and /eː/ and /oː/ in meet and boot had risen to /iː/ and /uː/. From around 1550, a second phase raised the vowels of mate, meat and boat.

slides.heading: Push or pull?
slides.text: Scholars still argue about the order. Did meet and boot rise first and push the old /iː/ and /uː/ out of place, or did those break up first and leave gaps that pulled the others up?

slides.question: In Northern English, one long vowel never became a diphthong. Which one?
slides.explanation: The /uː/ of house stayed put in the North. One explanation: Northern English had no /oː/ to rise into its place, because its /oː/ had already moved to the front of the mouth.

slides.heading: German respelled
slides.text: German went through similar vowel changes slightly earlier, but changed its spelling to match: Middle High German bīzen became modern beißen, ‘to bite’.
